title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI

st.t: Employment effects: Task substitution permits stable jobs
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that automation’s employment effects depend on the balance between displacement and productivity rather than following mechanically from task substitution. It materially develops that proposition through a task-based model showing how complementarities and new tasks can sustain labor demand, while separately explaining why output or physical productivity gains may yield limited wage and welfare gains.
qs: In this case,       new AI technologies would perform some of these subtasks and do so with sufficiently       high productivity, so that the subtask-level displacement would be weaker than the       productivity gains, expanding the demand for labor and the marginal productivity       of labor in these tasks.

Even though an increase in γL (z) raises the marginal physical product of labor, the equilibrium wage is determined by the value of the marginal product of labor, which depends on the adjustment of task prices.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source accepts that measured task-level gains do not establish worker displacement or economy-wide benefits, and materially extends the cluster by modeling those gains as conditional labour-cost savings while making explicit the assumptions about quality, task selection, complementarities and demand that govern any aggregate inference. It does not directly assess durable skill formation.
qs: Hence, from these experiments, we can only learn about the productivity gains, inclusive of any task complementarities—and not about the displacement effects.
As a baseline, I ignore the quality effects (which, as noted, are not uniform between the three studies) and focus on the average increase in speed and interpret this as average cost savings.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source accepts that observed gains are measure- and context-dependent: preliminary task-level experiments often favor lower-performing workers, but these results do not establish aggregate productivity or equitable economic distribution. It materially extends the cluster by distinguishing task-level cost savings from TFP and GDP effects and contrasting experimental gains with earlier automation’s adverse worker outcomes.
qs: Throughout, I distinguish between aggregate TFP and GDP (per capita/worker) effects, and I use productivity improvement at the micro/task level as synonymous to cost savings.

With previous automation technologies, such as robotics, most gains accrued to firm owners and managers, while workers in impacted occupations experienced negative outcomes (e.g., Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2020a).

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI gains are task-specific, that humans remain necessary for planning, checking and complementary work, and that context-dependent tasks resist extrapolation. It materially extends the cluster by supplying a task-weighted macroeconomic framework showing why selected productivity gains do not establish broad organisational, employment or welfare benefits, while stressing adjustment costs and uncertain labour reallocation.
qs: So long as AI’s microeconomic effects are driven by cost savings/ productivity improvements at the task level, its macroeconomic consequences will be given by a version of Hulten’s theorem: GDP and aggregate productivity gains can be estimated by what fraction of tasks are impacted and average task-level cost savings.

In hard problems, what leads to the desired outcome in a given problem is typically not known and strongly depends on contextual factors, or the number of relevant contexts may be vast, or new problem-solving may be required.

st.t: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
st.an: Acemoglu directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: aggregate gains depend on the economic share and cost savings of affected tasks, not raw task-level speedups alone. His estimates further show that difficult residual tasks, limited profitable adoption and organisational adjustment materially reduce projected productivity gains, while GDP and welfare may diverge.
qs: I show that when AI’s microeconomic effects are driven by cost savings (equiva- lently, productivity improvements) at the task level—due to either automation or task complementarities—its macroeconomic consequences will be given by a version of Hulten’s theorem: GDP and aggregate productivity gains can be estimated by what fraction of tasks are impacted and average task-level cost savings.
When the presence of hard tasks among those that will be exposed to AI is recognized, this upper bound drops to about 0.53%.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: Acemoglu directly supports the cluster’s central distinction: substantial task-level productivity gains do not establish employment effects, wage gains or reduced inequality. His macroeconomic modelling further reinforces the synthesis by projecting modest aggregate gains and showing that lower-skill productivity improvements can coexist with greater inequality.
qs: Hence, from these experiments, we can only learn about the productivity gains, inclusive of any task complementarities—and not about the displacement effects.
I show theoretically that even when AI improves the productivity of low-skill workers in certain tasks (without creating new tasks for them), this may increase rather than reduce inequality.

st.t: Junior hiring: Stable unemployment can hide adjustment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core distinction between task automation and employment displacement by modelling multiple productivity channels, including worker complementarity and specialisation after subtask automation. It does not provide evidence on unemployment stability or reduced junior hiring, so its support is theoretical and limited to the mechanisms mediating employment effects.
qs:  Task complementarity can increase the productivity in tasks that are not fully au-      tomated and may even raise the marginal product of labor.
Alternately, AI may automate some subtasks, while at the same time      enabling workers to specialize and raise their productivity in other aspects of their job.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core distinction between bounded task-level productivity gains and demonstrated worker displacement. It also reinforces the supervised-copilot framing by retaining human planning, debugging and checking, while cautioning that technical exposure and experimental gains do not establish economy-wide adoption or employment effects. It does not directly address legal apprenticeship risks.
qs: Hence, from these experiments, we can only learn about the productivity gains, inclusive of any task complementarities—and not about the displacement effects.

Overall performance will in- crease because of productivity effects, provided that this technology is better than/faster than humans at composing some subroutines (but humans are still needed for the other sub- tasks, including planning, debugging and checking).

kp.k: Task-level savings discipline aggregate AI productivity forecasts
kp.d: Acemoglu develops a task-based macroeconomic framework, primarily for the United States over approximately ten years, rather than a legal-sector analysis. Under competitive markets and constant returns to scale, a version of Hulten’s theorem links aggregate productivity improvements to the GDP-weighted share of affected tasks and their average cost savings. These are conditional theoretical relationships, not observed economy-wide AI effects.
qs: GDP and aggregate productivity gains can be estimated by what fraction of tasks are impacted and average task-level cost savings.

kp.k: Automation, complementarities, deepening, and new tasks differ
kp.d: The paper distinguishes AI taking over existing labor tasks, improving workers’ productivity in remaining tasks, improving already-automated tasks, and creating new tasks. Its quantitative estimates principally cover automation and task complementarities. It excludes transformative scientific advances from the ten-year calculations because the author considers large-scale effects unlikely within that horizon, rather than establishing that such effects are impossible.
qs: In this paper, I focus on the first two channels, though I also discuss how new tasks en- abled by AI can have positive or negative effects.
AI could induce deepening of automation—meaning improving performance

kp.k: Exposure does not establish profitable implementation
kp.d: Using Eloundou et al. (2023), Acemoglu sets tasks with 50% or less of their activities affected to zero, aggregates occupations using 2019–2022 US wage bills, and interprets the resulting 20% exposure share as a GDP share. He extrapolates Svanberg et al.’s computer-vision estimate that 23% of exposed tasks can be feasibly and profitably automated within ten years to the wider AI task set, yielding 4.6%. He explicitly acknowledges that this cross-technology extrapolation is consequential and unsupported by an equivalent non-computer-vision estimate.
qs: I set all tasks that the authors classify as having 50% or less of their activities impacted by AI and computer vision to zero
This procedure yields a wage bill-weighted share of exposed occupations equal to 20%.
This is not an innocuous step.

kp.k: Selected studies supply assumed task-level cost savings
kp.d: As reported in this May 2024 version, Noy and Zhang’s writing experiment found 40% faster completion and an 18% quality improvement; Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond’s customer-service rollout found approximately 14% faster completion, a slight statistically insignificant quality decline, and no improvement for the top quintile. Acemoglu averages the two speed estimates to assume 27% labor cost savings, ignores quality effects in the baseline, and applies an exposure-adjusted labor share of 0.535 to derive 14.4% overall savings. These assumptions translate selected task studies into macroeconomic inputs.
qs: They also estimate an 18% improvement in quality scores, as judged by peers and ChatGPT-based scoring of the output.
In fact, they estimate that the top quintile of associates experience no improvement at all.
Under these assumptions, the average labor cost savings are 27% (= 0.27).

kp.d: Peng et al. (2023) studied freelance programmers implementing an HTTP server on JavaScript with GitHub Copilot, then powered by OpenAI Codex (GPT-3). The paper reports 55.8% faster performance, but excludes this estimate from its baseline because the narrowly specified task had abundant training resources and may not generalize. Including it raises assumed average labor savings to 0.36 and overall savings to 0.193.
qs: They find that the treatment group performed the assigned tasks on average 55.8% faster than the control group.
If we add the numbers from Peng et al. to the mix, the average labor cost savings become 0.36, and thus the average overall cost savings come to 0.193.

kp.k: Task experiments cannot identify workforce displacement
kp.d: Acemoglu argues that productivity experiments assigning each participant a task cannot reveal whether employers subsequently need fewer workers. AI may perform drafting or programming subtasks while humans retain planning, debugging, checking, verification and modification. The ultimate labor-demand effect depends on displacement relative to productivity improvements and on substitution and product-demand elasticities.
qs: However, in this experimental setting, we do not see the displacement effects, because each of the treatment subjects are given the task and there is no possibility of reducing the number of workers performing this task.
Hence, from these experiments, we can only learn about the productivity gains, inclusive of any task complementarities—and not about the displacement effects.
but humans are still needed for the other sub- tasks, including planning, debugging and checking

kp.k: Baseline productivity gains are modest conditional projections
kp.d: Multiplying a 4.6% affected GDP share by 14.4% overall task savings produces a projected 0.66% cumulative TFP gain over ten years, approximately a 0.064% annual growth increment as stated in the paper. Including Peng et al. raises the cumulative estimate to 0.89%; raising feasible adoption to 30% of exposed tasks yields approximately 0.9%. Acemoglu contrasts these with much larger Goldman Sachs and McKinsey forecasts, but repeatedly describes his own figures as assumption-dependent, suggestive upper bounds.
qs: TFP gains over the next 10 years from AI are about 0.66%
If we were to consider the higher productivity numbers from Peng et al., 0.144 would be replaced by 0.193, and the 10-year TFP gains would be 0.89%, instead of 0.66%.
Nevertheless, these considerations make me conclude that even the 0.66% increase in TFP within the next 10 years due to AI is likely to be an upper bound on this technology’s medium-run effects.

kp.k: Learning difficulty limits extrapolation from early successes
kp.d: The author defines easy-to-learn tasks by observable success metrics and simple mappings from action to outcome. Hard-to-learn tasks involve contextual complexity, unclear outcomes or insufficient learning data, potentially preventing identification of expert human performance and limiting AI to average human behavior. This distinction concerns learning from outside observation, not human difficulty or the conventional routine/non-routine distinction.
qs: there is a reliable, observable outcome metric
there is a simple (low-dimensional) mapping between action and the outcome metric.
Crucially, “easy tasks” in this sense need not be easy for humans.

As a result, there will be a tendency for the performance of AI models to be similar to the average performance of human decision-makers, limiting the potential for large productivity improvements and cost savings.

kp.k: Hard-task adjustment reduces projected TFP to 0.53%
kp.d: The author assumes 7% labor savings for hard tasks versus 27% for easy tasks; this is a reasoned speculative choice, not a measured hard-task effect. His classification assigns 72.6% of wage-bill-weighted exposed tasks to the easy category, with affected easy and hard tasks comprising approximately 3.3% and 1.3% of GDP. Combining their respective overall savings of 0.144 and 0.037 yields a projected 0.53% cumulative TFP increase over ten years.
qs: it is impossible to know what their cost savings will be. Here I take those productivity gains to be 7%.
The end result is that 72.6% of wage bill-weighted exposed tasks in Eloundou et al. are easy.
When the presence of hard tasks among those that will be exposed to AI is recognized, this upper bound drops to about 0.53%.

kp.k: Task classification remains sample-bound and judgment-dependent
kp.d: The classification combines manually categorized verbs and Intermediate Work Activities, 100 latent topic clusters, and a gradient-boosted classifier for 4,089 exposed tasks. The main text reports a manually classified sample of 500, whereas the appendix reports 757; these are inconsistent descriptions within the supplied version. The appendix reports 90% agreement with training classifications and an AUC of 0.99, not independent evidence of generalization. The author warns against extending the classifier to non-exposed tasks and acknowledges that some writing tasks may be classified as too easy.
qs: We first manually classify a random sample of 500 exposed tasks as easy or hard.
We produce the training set by manually classifying 757 of the 4089 exposed tasks.
It matches 90% of the manual classification on our training data and has an AUC (area under the curve) score of 0.99.
Therefore, its output should not be directly extrapolated to non-exposed tasks.

kp.k: Adoption and organizational adjustment could lower gains
kp.d: Acemoglu cites evidence that fewer than 1.5% of US businesses invested in AI in 2019, arguing that adoption outside large firms may remain slow. He identifies possible monopolization and costly organizational adaptation as further constraints, invoking productivity J-curve research. These first two constraints are not incorporated into the adjusted numerical estimate; their omission supports his interpretation of the estimates as upper bounds.
qs: Acemoglu et al. (2022) estimate that less than 1.5% of US businesses had any investment in AI in 2019
If generative AI tools become monopolized in the hands of a few companies, this might further slow down their adoption by small and medium-sized firms.
Any major technology creates adjustment costs when adopted at large scale, because other organizational aspects need to evolve as well and this is typically quite costly and slow.

kp.k: Investment raises GDP beyond productivity, not equivalently welfare
kp.d: The conclusion reports cumulative ten-year GDP gains of 0.93%–1.16% under modest investment and 1.4%–1.56% with a larger investment response. The larger estimates assume capital adjustment completes within ten years and the required rate of return remains unchanged. Acemoglu distinguishes increased output from welfare: investment displaces consumption, while increased energy requirements can raise measured GDP without constituting a welfare benefit.
qs: the GDP boost within the next 10 years should also be modest, in the range of 0.93% − 1.16% over 10 years in total

This is under the assumption that all of the capital stock adjustment will take place within 10 years (while in practice it may take longer) and that the required rate of return on capital investments does not change
the GDP response would overstate the increase in consumer welfare, as investment comes at the expense of consumption

kp.k: Higher worker productivity need not deliver higher wages
kp.d: In the model, automation creates both a positive productivity effect and a negative displacement effect. Task complementarities also need not translate proportionately into wages: when tasks are gross complements, making a task easier can lower its price sufficiently to offset physical productivity gains. These conditional equilibrium mechanisms distinguish improved individual performance from increased market demand for that worker’s services; they are not direct empirical findings about legal wages.
qs: In general, this expression has ambiguous sign, so automation can increase or reduce wages.

Even though an increase in γL (z) raises the marginal physical product of labor, the equilibrium wage is determined by the value of the marginal product of labor, which depends on the adjustment of task prices.
Even when they increase wages, these technological shifts reduce the labor share, just like automation does

kp.k: Closing performance gaps can still increase wage inequality
kp.d: Acemoglu supplies a theoretical example in which AI disproportionately improves lower-skilled workers’ productivity in some tasks, yet raises wage inequality. Reduced demand for labor in those tasks reallocates workers into tasks where higher-skilled workers have a stronger comparative advantage. The argument establishes a possibility and cautions against inferring economy-wide distributional outcomes from within-task performance convergence.
qs: even a reduced productivity gap between low-skill and high-skill workers in some tasks could lead to greater inequality.

Hence, the overall inequality implications of AI cannot be directly deduced from its effects on the performance of workers of different skills in a given set of tasks and requires a fuller empirical exploration.

kp.k: Distributional projections reuse historical automation relationships
kp.d: The wage exercise covers 500 demographic groups differentiated by age, sex, race, education and immigration status, using 2018–2022 American Community Survey information. It imports a propagation matrix estimated for robots, software and dedicated machinery over 1980–2016, and assumes all quantified AI exposure becomes automation. Acemoglu acknowledges that historical ripple effects may not transfer to AI and that unequal task complementarities could change distributional results.
qs: The ripple effects estimated in Acemoglu and Restrepo (2022) may be context-specific
In this subsection, I ignore the task complementarities and presume that all of the AI exposure quantified so far will take the form of automation.
Estimates of the propagation matrix, Θ, are directly from Acemoglu and Restrepo (2022) and are for exposure to robots, software and dedicated machinery between 1980 and 2016.

kp.k: Projected gains favor capital without broadly equalizing wages
kp.d: The model finds AI exposure more evenly distributed across demographic groups than earlier automation, with the highest exposure among bachelor’s-degree and some-college workers and the lowest among workers without high-school qualifications. With hard tasks included, Table 1 projects average wages rising 0.77% and GDP 1.40% over ten years. The employment-weighted between-group standard deviation of log wages increases from 0.35 to 0.36, and capital’s income share rises about 0.31 percentage points. Low-education women, especially white native-born women, are projected to face real-wage declines despite positive averages for each education group.
qs: Workers with less than high school have the lowest exposure, followed by postgraduates, while workers with college degrees and those with associate degrees or some college have the highest exposure.
the between-group standard deviation of log wages (weighted by employment) increases slightly, from 0.35 to 0.36.
the capital share of national income increases by about 0.31 percentage points.

kp.k: New harmful tasks can separate GDP from welfare
kp.d: The paper discusses deepfakes, manipulation, addictive social media and malicious cyberattacks as potentially revenue-generating but socially harmful AI applications. Its explicitly speculative illustration uses Bursztyn et al.’s college-student social-media study: average willingness to pay to continue using platforms is $53 per user-month, while willingness to remove everyone in the network is $19. Applying that ratio to a hypothesized 2% of GDP in harmful activities gives the introduction and conclusion’s −0.72% consumption-equivalent welfare effect. Section 3.5 instead prints 0.072%, an internal numerical inconsistency. This is not a measured net welfare effect of AI.
qs: AI may generate new tasks that increase revenue, but reduce consumer utility
These considerations suggest that the numbers here should be taken as merely suggestive.
their impact on welfare may be −0.72%.

kp.k: New worker tasks offer a more beneficial pathway
kp.d: Within the model, new labor-intensive tasks can raise productivity, wages and labor’s income share; tasks directed toward lower-paid workers could also reduce wage inequality. Acemoglu excludes beneficial new-task gains from his numerical projections because they are difficult to measure, absent from the exposure sources, and—in his assessment—not current industry priorities. Their exclusion limits the scope of the estimates rather than demonstrating that such gains cannot occur.
qs: new tasks always increase wages and the latter always raises the labor share of national income as well

Productivity improvements from new tasks and new products, which have been impor- tant for previous transformative technologies, such as electricity and the Internet, are not incorporated into my estimates.
Rather, areas of pri- ority for the tech industry appear to be around automation and monetization of personal data

kp.k: Reliable contextual information should guide AI development
kp.d: Acemoglu recommends redirecting AI toward reliable, real-time information that expands workers’ expertise and problem-solving capabilities. His examples include electricians troubleshooting equipment and teachers identifying learning difficulties and personalizing instruction. He argues that larger benefits may require institutional, policy and regulatory changes, possibly alongside different model architectures, and questions whether general conversational foundation models are best suited to this objective.
qs: These tasks require real-time, context-dependent and reli- able information.
more beneficial outcomes may require new institutions, policies and regulations

it remains an open question whether we need foundation models (or the current kind of LLMs) that can engage in human-like conver- sations and write Shakespearean sonnets if what we want is reliable information useful for educators, healthcare professionals, electricians, plumbers and other craft workers.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Acemoglu predicts modest aggregate productivity gains from AI, limited wage gains, and a widening gap between capital and labor income; these are economy-wide claims rather than legal-sector forecasts.
pts.d: In the supplied May 2024 working paper, Acemoglu estimates a cumulative US TFP increase of approximately 0.66% over ten years from automation and task complementarities, reduced to approximately 0.53% when harder-to-learn tasks are incorporated. The conclusion reports cumulative GDP gains of 0.93%–1.16% with a modest investment response, or 1.4%–1.56% with a larger response. These are modeled increases relative to a baseline, not observed gains or annual growth rates. He argues that improved performance by lower-skilled workers in particular tasks does not necessarily reduce wage inequality because task prices, labor demand, and worker allocation also change. New labor-intensive tasks could produce larger productivity and wage benefits, but he considers their rapid emergence unlikely under current industry priorities. He also offers a highly speculative illustration in which harmful new activities increase measured GDP by 2% while reducing welfare by 0.72% in consumption-equivalent terms. Section 3.5 prints 0.072%, whereas the introduction and conclusion give 0.72%; this is an internal numerical inconsistency in the supplied text.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The forecasts combine a task-based economic model with existing exposure estimates and productivity studies, supplemented by explicitly speculative extrapolations.
pts.d: Acemoglu applies a version of Hulten’s theorem: aggregate TFP gains equal the GDP share of affected tasks multiplied by average task-level cost savings. He combines Eloundou et al.’s GPT-4-assisted occupational exposure estimates with BLS wage-bill data for 2019–2022 to estimate 20% exposure. Extrapolating Svanberg et al.’s computer-vision profitability estimate of 23% to broader AI gives 4.6% of tasks affected within ten years. The baseline averages Noy and Zhang’s writing-task result and Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond’s customer-service result into assumed labor cost savings of 27%, converted to 14.4% overall savings using industry labor shares. Peng et al.’s programming study enters a robustness check rather than the baseline. The hard-task adjustment uses manual classifications and machine learning to estimate 72.6% easy tasks among wage-bill-weighted exposed tasks, while assuming 7% labor cost savings for hard tasks. Distributional estimates reuse Acemoglu and Restrepo’s propagation estimates for automation during 1980–2016 with contemporary exposure and demographic data. The harmful-task illustration extrapolates Bursztyn et al.’s social-media willingness-to-pay experiment and selected platform revenues and cybersecurity spending; it is not a direct measurement of AI-caused welfare losses.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The main predictions concern approximately ten years from the 2024 analysis and are conditional on task-level cost savings, feasible adoption, and investment assumptions.
pts.d: Acemoglu treats the numbers as suggestive upper bounds rather than precise forecasts. The main estimates concern automation and complementarities in existing tasks, excluding revolutionary scientific effects and productivity gains from beneficial new tasks and products. Hard-to-learn tasks are expected to yield smaller gains because outcomes are difficult to observe and successful action depends on complex contextual information. Slow adoption, organizational adjustment costs, and possible concentration of AI provision could further reduce realized gains, but the numerical baseline does not incorporate all these constraints. The larger GDP estimates assume capital adjustment is completed within ten years and required returns do not rise. The distributional exercise treats measured exposure as automation and relies on historical spillover estimates whose applicability to AI is uncertain. Larger benefits remain possible if AI development shifts toward reliable, context-specific information, new worker tasks, and supporting institutional or policy changes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The analysis concerns US workers, capital owners, businesses and consumers, with uneven effects across demographic groups and potentially slower adoption by smaller firms.
pts.d: Acemoglu estimates that AI exposure is more evenly distributed across demographic groups than earlier automation. Workers with bachelor’s degrees and those with some college have relatively high exposure; workers without high-school qualifications have the lowest exposure, followed by postgraduates. In the hard-task-adjusted equilibrium model, average wages rise approximately 0.77% over ten years, compared with GDP growth of 1.4%, and the capital share rises approximately 0.31 percentage points. Education-group averages do not show substantial wage declines, but more detailed demographic estimates predict losses for low-education women, particularly white native-born women. Small and medium-sized businesses may adopt more slowly. Consumers may suffer from manipulative advertising, addictive social media, misinformation and malicious IT activity even when these generate revenue. Acemoglu identifies educators, healthcare professionals, electricians, plumbers and other workers as potential beneficiaries of a different AI development trajectory focused on reliable information and new tasks. He makes no distinct forecast for lawyers, law firms or legal clients.
